title: Varenicline for Youth Nicotine Vaping Cessation
abstract: Importance: Electronic cigarette use (vaping) among adolescents and young adults is common. Few treatments have been tested in this population. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of varenicline for nicotine vaping cessation in youth who do not smoke tobacco regularly. Design, Setting, and Participants: A 3-group randomized clinical trial compared 12 weeks of double-blind varenicline vs placebo, each added to brief, remotely delivered behavioral counseling and compared with single-blind enhanced usual care, with monthly follow-up to 24 weeks. The trial was conducted among youth, aged 16 to 25 years, who vaped nicotine daily or near daily, did not regularly smoke tobacco, and wanted to reduce or quit vaping, in a single US state from June 2022 to May 2024. Data collection ended May 28, 2024. Interventions: Participants were randomized (1:1:1) to 12 weeks of varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily over 7 days (standard titration), weekly counseling, and referral to text messaging vaping cessation support (This is Quitting [TIQ]) (n = 88); identical placebo, weekly counseling, and referral to TIQ (n = 87); or enhanced usual care (referral to TIQ only) (n = 86). Main Outcomes and Measures: Biochemically verified continuous vaping abstinence for the last 4 weeks of varenicline treatment vs placebo (primary outcome). Secondary outcomes included bioverified continuous abstinence from weeks 9 through 24 in the varenicline and placebo groups. Additional analyses compared varenicline group and placebo group with enhanced usual care. Results: Of 261 randomized participants (mean age, 21.4 years; 53% female), 254 completed the trial (97.3%). For varenicline and placebo, continuous abstinence rates were 51% vs 14% during weeks 9 through 12 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 6.5 [95% CI, 3.0-14.1]; P < .001) and 28% vs 7% during weeks 9 through 24 (aOR, 6.0 [95% CI, 2.1-16.9]; P < .001). Varenicline had higher continuous abstinence rates vs enhanced usual care during weeks 9 through 12 (51% vs 6%; aOR, 16.9 [95% CI, 6.2-46.3]) and during weeks 9 through 24 (28% vs 4%; aOR, 11.0 [95% CI, 3.1-38.8]). Continuous abstinence rates were not significantly different between the placebo and enhanced usual care groups. Study medication was generally well tolerated. Two varenicline participants (2%) and 1 placebo participant (1%) discontinued study medications due to adverse events. No drug-related serious adverse events occurred. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 76 (86%) in the varenicline group, 68 (79%) in the placebo group, and 68 (79%) in the enhanced usual care group. Conclusions and Relevance: Varenicline, combined with behavioral counseling, increased vaping abstinence in youth who vape nicotine and do not regularly smoke tobacco. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05367492.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This JAMA randomized clinical trial has already achieved notable scholarly traction, with 48 OpenAlex citations and a field-and-year standing in the top 1% most cited. The record also shows 49 documented downstream reuses and early uptake across addiction medicine, pediatrics, emergency medicine, and other clinical venues, suggesting the study has become an important reference point for youth nicotine vaping cessation.

Full narrative

Published in 2025, Varenicline for Youth Nicotine Vaping Cessation addresses a clear clinical gap: vaping is common among adolescents and young adults, yet few treatments have been tested in this population. The article reports a 3-group randomized clinical trial evaluating 12 weeks of double-blind varenicline versus placebo, alongside behavioral counseling, to assess cessation in youth who do not smoke tobacco regularly. Backed by NIDA and linked to a registered clinical trial, the study combines a timely intervention question with a rigorous trial design.

Its influence is visible in the citation record. OpenAlex shows 48 citations, and the article’s percentile standing places it in the top 1% for its field and publication year. That level of uptake is especially meaningful for a recent clinical trial and indicates that the paper is being used as evidence in the emerging literature on nicotine cessation, abstinence, and pharmacotherapy for young people.

The downstream literature suggests that the article is functioning as a reference point for synthesis rather than a single isolated result. It is cited in reviews and in new clinical studies spanning smoking cessation, substance use treatment, emergency department management of nicotine use, and youth-focused intervention development. The citing venues are concentrated in addiction and clinical medicine journals, including repeated appearances in journals such as Journal of Addiction Medicine, Substance Use & Misuse, JAMA, and JAMA Network Open, reinforcing its relevance to both specialty and broader medical audiences.

Beyond citation counts, the reuse record shows 49 downstream uses, mostly as research articles and reviews, with additional book-chapter and preprint reuse. Public discussion is comparatively quiet in the indexed record, with no event-data coverage captured, but the article does have limited podcast attention and repository visibility. Taken together, the evidence points to a paper that quickly moved into the scholarly conversation and is being used to shape how researchers and clinicians think about treatment options for youth nicotine vaping cessation.

The authorship and institutional footprint also support that trajectory, with contributors drawn from Harvard-linked institutions, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston Children’s Hospital, and the Medical University of South Carolina. In short, the study’s impact is currently best understood as strong academic and clinical uptake: a high-citation, high-reuse randomized trial that has already begun to anchor follow-on work on youth vaping cessation.
